decision: Use per-worker HMAC-SHA256 authenticated request envelopes with timestamp freshness, nonce replay protection, and existing fenced lease tokens for mission ownership

evaluatedApproaches.name: per-worker-hmac-envelope
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: authenticates worker identity and request integrity; binds workerId, action, timestamp, nonce, and payload into one signature
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: rejects tampering, replay, stale requests, wrong worker secrets, and stale lease owners when combined with DurableMissionQueue fencing
evaluatedApproaches.latency: one SHA-256 HMAC plus canonical serialization per request; negligible relative to filesystem queue mutation and future inter-VM transport
evaluatedApproaches.resourceUse: low; per-worker secret plus bounded in-memory nonce cache
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: medium-low because it wraps the existing queue API instead of changing mission semantics
evaluatedApproaches.qa: focused tests cover successful claim/complete, payload tamper rejection, nonce replay rejection, stale timestamp rejection, wrong-secret identity forgery rejection, and stale authenticated owner fencing

evaluatedApproaches.name: single-shared-hmac-secret
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: authenticates membership but cannot distinguish compromise of one worker from compromise of all workers
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: weaker blast-radius isolation and key rotation
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: low implementation complexity but materially weaker worker isolation
evaluatedApproaches.qa: rejected because one leaked worker secret would impersonate every worker

evaluatedApproaches.name: mutual-tls-per-worker
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: strong transport and worker authentication with mature certificate semantics
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: strongest long-term option when a dedicated coordinator transport and certificate lifecycle exist
evaluatedApproaches.latency: higher connection/setup overhead but acceptable with keepalive
evaluatedApproaches.resourceUse: higher operational complexity due to CA, issuance, revocation, rotation, and Qubes certificate provisioning
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: high for the current branch because no network transport contract exists yet
evaluatedApproaches.qa: deferred until the coordinator transport is selected

evaluatedApproaches.name: unsigned-local-transport
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: insufficient across trust boundaries because worker identity is only asserted, not proven
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: weak against impersonation and message modification
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: low implementation effort but unacceptable security risk for Qubes workers

whyItWon: It adds concrete worker authentication, integrity, freshness, replay resistance, and worker-specific blast-radius isolation now, while preserving the durable queue's fenced lease semantics and avoiding premature dependence on a particular Qubes transport. It is easy to replace or layer under mTLS later.
knownFailuresAndLessons: The nonce cache is process-local; a coordinator restart forgets seen nonces. Timestamp freshness limits the replay window, but REAL-WORKER readiness should persist replay state or use coordinator-issued sessions/counters.
HMAC authenticates messages but does not encrypt them. The eventual Qubes transport must provide confidentiality where mission contents are sensitive.
Secrets must never be committed to the repository. Qubes deployment needs per-worker secret provisioning and rotation through an isolated secret channel.
This protocol authenticates queue mutations only. Any external side effect still needs idempotency or resource-level fencing.
Canonical serialization is intentionally small and deterministic for JSON-compatible payloads; reject unsupported values at the transport boundary.

REAL-WORKER readiness still requires a concrete Qubes-safe transport, durable worker registry/session state, persistent replay protection or monotonic request counters, and multi-VM fault-injection metrics.
